what: Hancock Whitney is a regional bank along the US Gulf Coast, with branches across Mississippi, Louisiana, Alabama, Florida and Texas. It takes deposits and lends to businesses, commercial property owners and households, and runs trust and wealth-management services.
customers: Small and mid-sized businesses, energy and healthcare companies, commercial real-estate owners, consumers and wealth clients across the Gulf South.
money: The spread between loan and securities yields and the cost of deposits.
Trust and wealth management, deposit service charges, card fees and other income.
moat: Deep local relationships and a large share of deposits in its home markets, built over more than a century, which keeps funding cheap and loyal.
risks: The Gulf Coast economy is exposed to energy prices and hurricanes.
Commercial real-estate loans carry the usual regional-bank risk if property values fall.
Falling interest rates would compress the margin on its asset-sensitive balance sheet.
opportunities: Population and business growth in Texas and Florida markets expand lending opportunities.
Strong capital supports buybacks and dividend growth.
watch: Credit quality - net charge-offs and criticised loans. At this valuation the market is pricing in losses; if they do not arrive, the discount closes.
view: Hancock Whitney trades at about 12 times earnings and 3.1 times revenue, with the average analyst target about 33% above the price, which is a wide gap for a bank that earned $410 million and has grown revenue steadily from $1.3 billion to $1.5 billion. The market is applying a discount for two things that are real but probably overweighted: exposure to the energy economy and the hurricane risk of the Gulf Coast.

The bank was badly hurt in the 2015-16 oil downturn, when energy loans went bad, and investors have long memories. Since then it has shrunk its energy book, diversified into healthcare and commercial lending, and kept a conservative balance sheet. Its deposit franchise in Mississippi and Louisiana is cheap and stable, and that is what earns a regional bank its returns over a full cycle.

I think the discount is wider than the risks justify. The thing that would prove me wrong is a turn in credit: if criticised loans rise or commercial property losses appear, the low multiple is deserved. Absent that, this is a well-run, well-capitalised bank priced as if trouble were coming, and the combination of a low multiple and steady buybacks gives owners a reasonable return while they wait.
bull: Credit stays clean, the Gulf economy keeps growing, and steady buybacks plus a re-rating close much of the gap to the analyst target.
bear: An energy downturn or a major hurricane season hits loan quality, and falling rates squeeze the margin at the same time.
